utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Chester Stamp, Ekkehard Withopf, and Ruth Karper, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; and Muriel Cauvin, my legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and our legal assistant, Mr. Mulalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present in the courtroom, the members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, the registrar, who has joined us for this hearing, the usher, and everyone else present in the courtroom. And I wouldn't want to forget the interpreters either. We have a witness scheduled for today, but I will first give the floor to the Defence, who have had the opportunity to reflect on the matter over the weekend and are now in a position to tell us about their position with regard to our decision rendered last week, which concerns the documents and documents that were contested. The Prosecution may make comments after the Defence has taken the floor, but could the Defence tell us what the situation is at present.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. On behalf of both Defence teams, we wish to thank Your Honours firstly for the opportunity you have given us to consider your decision over the weekend. Our requests today, following in-depth discussions about the matter, is that Your Honours consider varying to some degree the decision that Your Honours rendered on Friday last week. Our proposal is, Your Honours, that we as the Defence teams are not required to give our detailed reasons why we object to the documents at this stage. The date which Your Honours gave was the 8th of April or -- or one week later but that we are given until the end of the Prosecution case to outline what our objections are. In the interim, Your Honours, we propose that all of the documents are marked for identification - that's the contested documents - that they are available to the Court and to the parties, and that in the two months that remain of the Prosecution case, the Prosecution seek to introduce as many of those documents through witnesses who do attend. In addition, the expert witness, General Reinhardt, will have an opportunity to refer to those documents that are relevant that are marked for identification. And at the end of that process, we then reassess how many documents have still not been admitted and that the Prosecution then have an opportunity to address Your Honours on which documents they still wish to rely upon and tender into evidence. It is correct, Your Honours, that the jurisprudence of the Tribunal does not require a witness to be available to introduce each and every document. There are many examples from other cases where documents have been admitted without the presence of a witness. But at the same time that the jurisprudence does indicate that where possible, and as far as possible, documents should be introduced through witnesses, and if not, then the practice has been, Your Honours, for the Prosecution to outline to the Trial Chamber which documents they wish to rely upon, making legal arguments as to their relevancy and their reliability, with the Defence then being given an opportunity to respond and the Trial Chamber rendering its decision thereafter. And our proposal would be that with the remaining documents which haven't been tendered through witnesses at the end of the Prosecution case some time is set aside for the parties to address Your Honours on which documents should still be admitted. The Prosecution would then have a chance to go through the documents category by category, which has been the -- the practice in other cases, not to admit documents wholesale but for the Prosecution to be required to explain category by category - for example, if documents came from a government office, to explain the source of those documents, the relevance of them, why the Prosecution believes they are reliable, and for the Defence in light of those submissions to then respond, and for Your Honours then to rule on which documents should be admitted. So the -- the net result, Your Honour, our proposal is that we not be required to state what our objections are now because many witnesses might still be coming who can introduce these documents and we then have the opportunity to cross-examine them and set out our objections, and that at the end of the case, when we know exactly what is left over, the Prosecution can outline what is the relevance of the remaining documents, the reliability of those documents, if they to introduce them, and we can then respond, in accordance with Your Honours' ruling that we then set out what are our particular objections. Your Honours, we will, if you so request, set out our arguments in writing and indicate what the jurisprudence is, if that could be of assistance to Your Honours. We don't wish to delay the matter any further. But if Your Honours are not in agreement with the proposal that we are putting forward - and further motivation is required - we can in the next few days, certainly by the end of our session on Thursday, submit our arguments in more detail in writing. The Prosecution could also submit their arguments in response at the same time or be given some further time to -- to respond. And then a decision could be rendered. But we've outlined our basic proposal today, so Your Honours are aware of what consideration we have given to the matter. In our submission, such a proposal would be a much more practical way, firstly, of resolving a situation which involves many hundreds of documents, and not just a handful, but hundreds of documents; and secondly, and most importantly, it would ensure that the rights of the accused are properly protected in that, firstly, the Defence would be given an opportunity to cross-examine witnesses who are introducing documents. And if witnesses cannot attend, be given an opportunity to respond to what the Prosecution is submitting regarding the relevance and reliability of those documents. And the burden would remain on the Prosecution to present its case, with the Defence having to respond, which is the way in which proceedings are conducted before this Tribunal. Your Honours, lastly we wanted to -- to point out for the record, because this was mentioned last week, that it is correct that the Prosecution has indicated in their pre-trial brief which documents they seek to rely upon and what the relevance of those documents is. We have looked at the pre-trial brief carefully and have calculated that only 222 of the documents mentioned in the pre-trial brief are in the consolidated list of documents, and of those we have already admitted 95, leaving 127 documents which the Prosecution have given the Defence proper notice of regarding how they seek to use those documents to prove their case. So that's 127 documents of the over-600 documents that we are on notice as to how the Prosecution seeks to rely upon them. But doing the calculations, Your Honours will see that that leaves over 500 documents which we do not know what reliance the Prosecution wishes to place on them. We also in many instances are not aware of what the source of those documents is and how those documents Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were gathered. They are not even, in many instances, basic chain of custody statements as to who obtained the documents, when they were obtained, and how they were handed to the Prosecution. So we would be in a position, Your Honour, to respond to that small number of documents, the 127, but not the bulk of the documents, over 500. And in our view, it would be a much more practical solution to look at all of the contested documents together by, first of all, seeing what witnesses can introduce them, and then dealing with the remaining documents category by category thereafter. We should also not forget, Your Honours, that the Defence, when it presents its case, might well refer to many of these documents as well, which could allow them to be introduced that way, depending on the nature of the Defence case. And, of course, Your Honours have the opportunity to call witnesses who might be relevant to these documents at the end of the case. So it is a process that can continue beyond the Prosecution case if necessary. Your Honour, those are our submissions. It's an oral application for Your Honours to consider varying the order that has been made. But as I have mentioned, it can be formalised in writing with all the arguments if Your Honours would prefer that method and if that could be of assistance in resolving this matter. Thank you, Your Honours, again for the opportunity to revisit the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to Mr. Withopf, there is something I would like to Defence to clarify for me. You said that in their pre-trial brief 222 documents were mentioned. There are 95 documents which are not problematic, in your opinion, and there are 127 documents which raise certain issues. As far as the 95 documents are concerned, the ones that you say are admissible, have those documents already been included in the list of documents that you have approved of, or are these 95 new documents? Are these different documents? Or have these 95 documents already been included among the 200 documents that are not being contested?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the 95 documents are already included in the 286 documents that the Defence is prepared to admit at this stage, so they are already included in that -- that number. And 127 are documents that are not included, that are still contested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dixon. I'll now give the floor to Mr. Withopf to hear what his position is, and then the Trial Chamber will assess the matter. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution's response to the submission of the Defence will be comprised of three sections. It appears to be necessary to very briefly summarise what has happened in the past in order to show where we were on Friday last week. I will then address the legal principles and the legal considerations of motions for reconsideration. And even if Defence phrases it differently, the today's motion is a motion for reconsideration of the Trial Chamber's decision of last Friday. Then, Your Honours, Mr. President, I will provide the Chamber with a number of additional facts which may help the Chamber to determine on the motion for reconsideration, as put forward today by the Defence. Where were we on Friday, Friday last week at the point the Trial Chamber made it decision? The Prosecution has a consolidated exhibit list, and the consolidated exhibit list has 966 documents on the list. 663 of such documents are contested by the Defence, meaning more than 65 per cent. In respect to the reasons why they do contest such documents, Defence has given very general reasons in their filing of 13th of March, Tuesday last week, mainly outlining - and I'm referring to paragraph 3 - that there are two reasons, authenticity or relevance, and in some cases both of such reasons, and Defence is then providing the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber with additional 12 criteria which may impact on these two reasons, and they are emphasising that these are criteria inter alia. The Chamber has decided on Friday the Defence at the very latest by 15th of April should provide the Chamber and the Prosecution the grounds for contesting the documents and that the Prosecution has to respond a week later. This decision, Your Honour, was based on the Trial Chamber's consideration that - and I quote - that: "Introducing documents solely through witnesses would result in a considerable extension of the time needed for hearing witnesses and would have adverse effects on the efficiency of the process of the proceedings." The Defence on Friday has asked to readdress this issue after a number of different indications were given as to how they wish to readdress this issue. It turned out, as the Prosecution has already anticipated on Friday, that it is a motion for reconsideration. What Defence want is not varying the decision in the one -- in respect to the one or the other minor issue. They wish to have the motion being reconsidered and being reconsidered along the lines they had addressed earlier on in these proceedings. Motions for reconsideration, Mr. President, Your Honours, motions for reconsideration do not form part of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the International Tribunal. They have no basis in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. And I refer to the Celebici Appeals Chamber decision of 1st of June, 1999 in which this issue has been addressed in some length. That means, Mr. President, Your Honours, that only in very -- in very particular circumstances a Trial Chamber can be asked to reconsider one of its decisions. Such particular circumstances, Mr. President, Your Honours, have been detailed by the jurisprudence of this International Tribunal as, "A change of circumstances," number one; and number two, "A change of circumstances resulting in the previous decision being erroneous and causing prejudice to the accused." These principles, Mr. President, Your Honours -- this principle applied to the present case show -- this principle shows that the Defence motion for reconsideration has no basis in law. There is no change of circumstances, Mr. President, Your Honours. The Prosecution exhibit list is very well known to the Defence. The exhibits themselves are known to the Defence. The majority of these exhibits has been disclosed many months ago. Many of them actually have been disclosed more than two years ago. And the issue has been discussed repeatedly and in each and every detail since the beginning of these proceedings. The Defence has had ample -- has had ample opportunity to address all the issues they addressed today in oral -- in both in oral and in written submissions. Secondly, the Trial Chamber's decision is not erroneous. The procedure applied by this Trial Chamber - namely, the tendering of the documents into evidence from the bar table and not via witnesses - this is not only a well-established procedure in civil law jurisdictions and a well-established practice in such jurisdictions; it has also been applied repeatedly -- it has been applied repeatedly before this International Tribunal. And I'm referring to the cases of the Prosecutor versus Simic and the Prosecutor versus Galic. As a result, the Defence motion has no basis in law. The motion for reconsideration has no basis in law. Already for this reason, the Prosecution submits that the Defence motion should be denied. In the event, however, Mr. President, Your Honours, that the Trial Chamber doesn't share this view, as just detailed by the Prosecution, I wish to provide the Chamber additional facts to finally determine this issue. Defence has identified, as already mentioned, two main criteria: Authenticity and relevance. And they had identified, inter alia, as they are saying, additional 12 factors which impact on such criteria. They did not show which of these two criteria apply to which document. They even said that in some cases both criteria may apply, and of course and consequently, they did not inform which of the 12 factors may apply to the different sorts of documents. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Since the Defence, Mr. President, Your Honours, were able to identify the two reasons and they were even able to identify the 12 factors, one would have thought that they have carefully considered the issue document by document and that they would have been able to inform both the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber what the problems and what the challenges to the documents may be. They haven't done so. On Friday after the Trial Chamber rendered its decision - and I really wish to emphasise that last week this issue prior to rendering the decision has been again and in great detail discussed - Defence counsel informed both the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution - and that's now a quote; and I'm referring to page 111552 and 111559 of the Friday's transcript - that: "It would require more than two weeks of work to make our first assessment without drafting anything." That means it would be the first assessment. This statement, Your Honours, Mr. President, leaves the Prosecution with the question how were they able -- how were Defence able to identify the documents which they were contesting and which they were not contesting if Defence hasn't made even -- hasn't even made its first assessment? In respect to the facts, I wish to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber of a number -- on a number of issues. 375 documents which were contested stem from the so-called Sarajevo collection. Mr. President, Your Honours, the Sarajevo collection is a collection of documents seized as a result of a consensual search of the ABiH main archive in Sarajevo. These are official documents that were kept in the official ABiH main archive in Sarajevo. The Chamber, Mr. President, Your Honours, you may be interested to know that 72 per cent out of these documents have been contested by the Defence; 308 of the Sarajevo collection exhibits are 3rd Corps documents; 204 are contested; 148 of such documents are 7th Muslim Brigade documents; 138 are contested, meaning 93 per cent; and there are many more. More than 300 of such documents actually stem from the ABiH 3rd Corps, and these are documents that are relevant to the time period of the indictment. More than 100 of such documents - namely, 104, Mr. President, Your Honours - show that the accused Hadzihasanovic is the originator of such documents. More than 50 of such documents show that the accused Kubura is the originator of these documents. Mr. President, Your Honours, taking into account that these documents stem from the official ABiH main archive, they were seized as a result of a search operation which was done in consensus with the Bosnian authorities, and that they show both of the accused as the originators of these documents, it would be very helpful for the Prosecution and for the Trial Chamber to get to know the reasons why Defence are contesting these documents. And in this context, Mr. President, Your Honours - and I'm coming to the end of my oral submissions - I wish to draw the attention on two of these 12 factors which have been detailed by my learned colleagues from the Defence side, which are, just an example, since I don't want to waste the Court's time -- which are just an example, what would it mean if the Court were to reconsider its decision from last Friday. There is the issue of signature, and there is the issue of problems with translation. If the signature on a document is challenged by the Defence, this of course would involve a number of efforts - and everybody in this courtroom is knowing what I am talking about - would involve a number of efforts which would significantly delay the court proceedings, which would delay this trial, since we would need an expert if there are issues with the signature. And the expert would need to get examples, and he would have to compile his report, and he would have to submit the report, and the report would have to be translated. Obviously this would cause a serious delay of the proceedings. Even more of concern, however, Mr. President, Your Honours, is the factor which is identified by the Defence as problems with translation. As already mentioned earlier on, Defence, since a substantial period of time, is in possession of most of the vast majority of the documents themselves which are on the exhibit list, and they got the translations and they were able to assess any translation problems. And Defence is the only party which is able to assess translation problems, since we are not speaking B/C/S we have to rely on what we get from CLSS, and there's no reason for the Prosecution to have any doubt that what we get from CLSS is the absolute correct translation. What Defence is asking for - and I really wish to emphasise this - would result in the following situation: There is a witness the Prosecution wishes to -- wishes the witness to comment on a certain document. The document is shown to the witness. Defence raises an issue in respect to problems with translation. Nobody in the courtroom other than Defence is in a position to identify where the problems are. The problems - and I do appreciate the position of the Defence, that sometimes it may be very necessary to have a 110 per cent accurate translation - that would mean even the best qualified translator in the courtroom may not be in a position to translate it on the spot. It would have to be re-given to CLSS, the concerns of the Defence would have -- would have to be taken into account, the witness would have to be sent home, the witness would have to be recalled at a later point in time, and the document would have to be shown to the witness again. Since Defence is not volunteering to us at this point in time to give an indication which documents are concerned and which documents -- and what are the problems with translations, such a situation we may face with each and every witness in the near future. We don't know, since Defence is not telling us. And the Prosecution doesn't want to speculate on the reasons why not. The burden of proof has been addressed by my learned colleagues from the Defence side. If the Defence follows the procedure as established by the Court decision of last Friday, the burden of proof isn't touched upon at all, since it's obviously still the Prosecution who has to address the issue of authenticity, who has to satisfy the Trial Chamber about the relevance of the documents, and it's still the Prosecution who has to show that the other 12 factors are met. To summarise the Prosecution's submission, Mr. President, Your Honours, number one, Defence had ample opportunity over the past months, and they did so, to address all related issues in order to inform -- to give the Trial Chamber a chance to make an informed decision. The motion for reconsideration as such has no basis in the Tribunal's law, nor in the Tribunal's jurisprudence. And number three, if the motion for reconsideration would be granted for the reasons I outlined - and I really wish to emphasise that I don't want to waste the Court's time; I could make such submissions in respect to each and every of the 12 factors Defence mentioned - if the Trial Chamber would grant the Defence motion for reconsideration, it can be anticipated that this trial -- that the duration of this trial will be substantially - will be substantially - longer. Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. I give the floor once again very briefly to Mr. Dixon, and then we will stop the discussion on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I will take it very quickly. Thank you. The main point that we wish to make, Your Honour, is that we are not trying to avoid making our objections known on these various documents. It's only in the interests of the accused to make sure that our objections are conveyed and clearly stated for the record. Our position is that at this stage it would not be practical for us to be putting forward our objections in detail when it's not clear from the Prosecution side how they wish to rely upon many of these documents. My learned friend very successfully outlined the way the procedure could work when he, for example, started addressing the Sarajevo collection, setting out which documents are part of that collection, how were they collected, how were they to be relied upon. I don't wish to in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. any way suggest how the Prosecution could address this matter further, but it would be open to the Prosecution to call a witness or witnesses regarding that collection, and many of the documents could then be addressed through such a witness, giving the Defence an opportunity to cross-examine as to how documents were collected, how were they sent to this archive. And in that way, to test the reliability of those documents. As my learned friend from the Prosecution has indicated, the burden does rest on the Prosecution, and our simple request is not to change Your Honours' decision. We of course have to respond by indicating what our objections are. But in our view, it would be a much better course for the Prosecution first to outline through their witnesses and through their oral submissions, like my learned friend has done, what relevance they place on these documents and at a minimum to show what are the indicia of reliability, and then the Defence, as Your Honours have ordered, would be in a position to respond. And at that point, at the end of the Prosecution case a ruling can be made as to what documents would be admitted. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to refer to some of the arguments submitted by my learned friend, drawing attention to the legal situation with regard to the request for the reconsideration of the ruling. Reviewing your decision of Friday, the Defence was confronted with a problem that we presented before you, Your Honours, and that is that the consistent implementation of such a decision within the deadlines you have set could result in the basic rights of the accused being infringed upon, and that is one of the arguments that colleague Withopf referred to, that is, that it was in accordance with the jurisdiction of this Tribunal, that one of the grounds for reconsideration is based on the rights of the accused. The Defence relies on Articles 20 and 21 of the Statute. It is true that Article 20 of the Statute draws attention to the importance of expedition and fair trial for the accused. The arguments presented by my learned friend Withopf draws attention to only one of the two elements, and that is the problems that would be provoked by such a decision regarding expeditiousness. However, we wish to draw attention to the other aspect, that is, the fair trial and respect for the rights of the accused, as guaranteed by Article 21 of the Statute. As my learned colleague Mr. Dixon has said, we believe that one of the basic rights of the accused is the right to cross-examine. That is why the jurisdiction of this Tribunal, fully acknowledging the need that the Prosecution may tender documents without necessarily using a witness to do so, the general practice has been for a witness to be brought for the purpose of tendering documents so that the Defence can, of course, cross-examine. Secondly, which we consider to be very important, we looked at your decision of the 24th of February, and we reviewed the procedure we have applied in the past four months, and it is our submission that the objections of the Prosecution to Defence exhibits prompted your rulings, which meant that only 26 Defence documents were identified -- marked for identification only. Also on the basis of our objections, only 13 Prosecution documents have been marked for identification, because it was your opinion, Your Honours, that documents needed to be tendered in an appropriate manner. The next argument proffered by the Prosecution in challenging our right to have documents tendered in the way suggested by my colleague is that the Defence has had in its possession most of these documents for more than two years. For clarification purposes, I wish to say that it was through a request for access to the archives that the Defence obtained access to these documents, but this was access to the archives and not through disclosure. The total archives of the 3rd Corps of the Supreme Command and the 7th Muslim Brigade were exempted from the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina and were no longer to be found there but were in the possession of the Prosecution of this Tribunal. For this reason, the Defence was granted access to these documents. I also wish to remind you, Your Honours, that the Prosecution was duty-bound to provide us with a consolidated list on the 10th of October together with their pre-trial brief; however, you are aware that we received that list much later, following repeated insistence by the Trial Chamber. I wish also to go back to one of the basic rights of the accused, and that is to be informed in his own language of all the charges against him. That is why it is our position that the Prosecution should be obliged to state how each document relates to the case and the charges, and the grounds for tendering them, explaining also their authenticity and relevance. As colleague Dixon has already said, on the consolidated list, there are more than 500 documents for which the Prosecution has not linked them to the case in the indictment. And now the Defence is being asked to take a position on these documents, which means that we would have to state our views on documents in advance before knowing the significance that the Prosecution attaches to them and their relevance to the case. Furthermore, in connection with the translations, we never had in mind the translations which contain minor errors. As we have already informed the Prosecution, we today have about 40 documents on the consolidated list which were never provided to the Defence in translation. And one of the basic rights of the accused, according to Article 21 of the Statute, is that he has to have all those documents in his own language. For these reasons, Your Honours, it was our view that we shouldn't spend your time and the time of all of us here in the courtroom to set out all these arguments in detail, as well as the jurisdiction and jurisprudence of this Tribunal. If we had been asked to do so in writing, we would have done so if that were to be of any use to you. If you are going to render a decision today about our oral motion, our final proposition would be that we admit 286 documents not contested by the Defence, that we continue to admit into evidence other documents through witnesses in the same way that we have been doing so far, and that eventually the Prosecution, as in many other cases, should, depending on the needs of its own case, set forth the arguments, the grounds, on the basis of which they need other documents, and only then, upon receiving such reasoned explanation, would the Defence be able to respond. I think we would not only gain in terms of expeditiousness, but also this trial would meet the other basic criterion, and that is respect for the rights of the accused and a fair trial. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we envisaged, that you should only have the right to respond once - you have responded twice - so the Prosecution will also be given the floor to respond to what you have just said, and then we will stop there. I would just like to ask the Prosecution to provide us some additional information regarding two points that were raised by the Defence, and that is that 40 documents have still not been translated; and secondly, regarding the totality of the documents on the consolidated list, I counted more than 800. 860. And out of the 860 documents, only 222 apparently will be -- were included in the pre-trial brief. That is what we are told by the Defence. And proceeding from there, there would be about 600 documents which are not referenced in the pre-trial brief. So, Mr. Withopf, just in a few minutes I give you the floor, and after that we will hear the witness. The Chamber will make its ruling and let you know tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, just very briefly answering the Court's questions. Defence has submitted to us a list containing 40 out of the 966 Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. documents which are not yet translated. The Prosecution is taking care of this issue. We will examine the list. It can be anticipated that most, if not all of these documents, are actually not yet translated. The Prosecution will take care of this issue and will provide Defence with translations of such documents at the very earliest opportunity. I wish, however, in this context to emphasise that Defence counsel are speaking both languages, English and B/C/S, and that they are able to provide the two accused with a translation of documents if they are in English into B/C/S. However, if there's a problem, the Prosecution will take care of it. The Prosecution has also examined how many documents are referred to in the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. The Prosecution's pre-trial brief is actually exceptionally detailed in making reference to documents and it has done so in great detail, far beyond the usual practice before this Tribunal. The Prosecution has counted the referenced documents as well. The number is similar to the number as put forward by the Defence. This is certainly not at issue. We counted some 254 documents. However, Defence was in possession of the exhibit list three days after the filing of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, and the delay was actually caused by an agreement Defence and the Prosecution had for the reason the Defence wanted to have the exhibits in an electronic version. It was an agreement by both parties. Again, this is certainly not at issue. My learned colleague from the Hadzihasanovic Defence was emphasising the issue of the consolidated exhibit list. This is, again, not an issue because Defence had two exhibit lists. The consolidated exhibit list is nothing else but having merged two exhibit lists in one list. It doesn't mean that there were many more additional documents. Defence knew by mid-October about the vast majority of the documents the Prosecution is relying upon as evidence in this case. The Sarajevo collection, if I may address this issue - and again, this issue has been discussed at length in the course of the many Rule 65 ter meetings and Status Conferences. And I refer to the transcripts of such meetings and conferences. The Sarajevo collection was earlier on provided to the Defence in its whole; meaning, more than 50.000 pages of documents in electronic version. The Prosecution has done far more than it was required under the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Under the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Prosecution was only required to disclose Rule 68 materials and to disclose Rule 66(A)(i) and (A)(ii) materials. The Prosecution has done everything to enable the Defence to have the Sarajevo collection very early on in electronic version, the full collection. At the very end of my submissions, Mr. President, Your Honours, I think that many of the arguments put forward by the Defence distract from the focus of the Chamber's decision of last Friday. The focus of the Chamber's submission [sic] of last Friday was to keep the proceedings focussed and to allow both parties to proceed in the same pace, in the same quick pace as they did in the past. The Prosecution again expresses its serious concerns that in the event the Defence motion for reconsideration is granted, this will result in a serious delay of proceedings. My learned colleagues have already indicated - and that's certainly correct - that the Prosecution would be forced to call additional witnesses, and then -- for example, for the Sarajevo collection, that would mean that more than 350 documents would have to be put to this one witness, and Defence may raise objections in respect to each and every of the documents. It's hardly to imagine how many days, if not weeks, such a procedure would need to be finished. It appears to be far better to proceed as has been decided by the Trial Chamber on Friday; namely, to stick to the decision, to not reconsider the decision, and to order the Defence that they have to come forward with their challenges. It's a bit odd that they say to us, "At the very end of the proceedings we will explain what the challenges are about, and now Prosecution, at the very end of the Prosecution case, now you are obliged to bring additional witnesses to address issues of authenticity, to address issues of signature, and to address the many other issues which have been detailed in the Defence written submission of 30th of March this year." Again, the Prosecution wishes this oral motion for reconsideration -- for reconsideration being dismissed. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will render our decision at the hearing tomorrow, with respect to the oral motion asking the Chamber to reconsider its oral ruling of last Friday. We have a witness planned for today. Before bringing the witness in, I should like to say that tomorrow the hearing will begin at 2.15, simply for reasons linked to a plenary that will be held at 5.00 p.m. So we will have a break at 5.00 p.m., and then we will resume at 6.00 p.m. So tomorrow there will be a break between 5.00 and 6.00 in the afternoon, because there is a plenary meeting of the Judges of this Tribunal at that time. Mr. Usher, will you go and bring the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Let me first check that you can hear what I am saying in your own language. If so, please tell me so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber welcomes you, and we wish to tell you that you have been called as a witness by the Prosecution and because you're going to testify, you need to take the solemn declaration. But before you do that, I need to identify you, so will you please give me your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am Sead Zeric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when were you born, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 31st of July, 1957.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a graduate lawyer, and I work in the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a lawyer in the judiciary. But more specifically, what is your exact position? Are you working in the Ministry of Justice or in a court? Will you tell us what your exact position is now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am deputy district prosecutor for Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in 1993, more than ten years ago, what was your position in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was district military prosecutor in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified in an international or national court on the events of 1993, or is this the first time that you are being asked to testify in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Will you be kind enough to read the solemn declaration, please. Mr. Usher will give it to you. Please read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As you are a prosecutor, you are surely familiar with the way in which proceedings are conducted before this Tribunal. I'll provide you with certain information about the procedure that will be followed here. Initially you will be examined by the Prosecution. The Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. representatives of the Prosecution are to your right. They represent this Tribunal's OTP. Once they have completed their examination-in-chief, Defence counsel, who are to your left, will conduct their cross-examination. Perhaps you know them. They are to your left. In addition, the three Judges sitting before you may at any point in time, if they believe that it might be useful, ask you questions that relate to the questions put to you by the Prosecution or the Defence, or we may ask you questions if we believe that it is necessary to obtain additional information, to fill in any gaps that there may be in your answers. As you have made a solemn declaration, this means that you should speak the truth. And in the case of giving false testimony, and witness may be prosecuted for having given false testimony. This is a purely academic question, given your position. A second matter that has to do with the procedure that is followed in this Tribunal concerns the fact that if a witness provides information that could at a subsequent date be used against that witness, in such a case the witness may refuse to answer the question. This is a procedure followed in common-law countries, but it also exists in countries where continental law is in force. But if the witness refuses to reply, the Trial Chamber can compel the witness to answer the question. In such a case the witness has a certain form of immunity, in that the information that the witness provides can't be used against the witness. So this is the manner in which the proceedings will be conducted. Given your position, you will be answering the questions fully and precisely. There will be questions that you will have to answer, questions that will be put to you by the Prosecution. You will have to provide them with detailed answers. And then the Defence will ask you questions. And very often when the Defence conducts its cross-examination, the answers might simply be yes or no. When the Judges ask you questions, the questions put to you will be very precise, and you will provide the appropriate answers in such a case. Roughly speaking, this is how the proceedings will be conducted. Without wasting any more time - because we only have a half an hour before the break - I'll now give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President and Your Honours. And good afternoon. And good afternoon to you too, Mr. Zeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: First, could you tell us, please, when were you appointed the district military prosecutor for Travnik.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: I became the district military prosecutor on the 22nd of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And can you briefly, by way of introduction, just outline your professional career up until that point.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: When I graduated in 1980 at the Faculty of Law, after graduating, I worked in an educational institute for four or five years. And then from -- and then from 1995 until the beginning of the war, I worked in Travnik municipality. I performed various duties and held various positions. I spent the largest period of time as the main inspector in the sector for protection -- defence and protection in Travnik. On the 22nd of December, 1992, I was appointed as the -- as I have already said, district military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As district military prosecutor for Travnik, which court did you work in and when was that court established?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: I didn't work in a court, because the prosecutor was a separate organ. It was independent of the court. And that organ was founded in 1992 for the first time -- or rather, in December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that was the district military court for Travnik?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: The district military prosecutor's office. The district military court was a separate organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the district military court in Travnik had jurisdiction for which geographical areas?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Well, the geographic area corresponded, roughly speaking, to canton number 6, the Central Bosnia canton. That's from Kiseljak, Fojnica, Busovaca, Vitez, Novi Travnik, Travnik, Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf, and Jajce. That would be the area that it covers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what was the subject matter jurisdiction? And by that, I mean what types of offences or crimes did the district military court in Travnik have jurisdiction over?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Well, it had jurisdiction -- the district court in Travnik or the district prosecutor's office had jurisdiction for all crimes, all first-level crimes committed by military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the -- your office, the district prosecutor's office, to which government agency did it belong? That is, which ministry or government agency was it subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: I think it was to the Ministry of Justice at the time, and we were directly linked to the Ministry of Justice of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in terms of organisational structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. The criminal cases that the court had a jurisdiction over, how were these cases initiated? In other words, tell us about the system, how a case came before the prosecutor's office and before the court.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Well, the procedure was the usual one followed according to our criminal law. All organs, all persons could file a criminal report against anyone who had perpetrated a crime. Naturally, natural persons were in a position to file such reports too. Most frequently reports were filed by the civilian police, by the military police, by individual brigades, corps, et cetera. It was very seldom done by natural persons; although, such cases did exist too. Having received a criminal report, the Prosecution would examine it and decide whether they should institute proceedings or not if -- or continue with proceedings or not. If there was sufficient evidence to continue with proceedings, we would follow the law on criminal procedure at the time, and we would take measures provided for by the law. In individual cases, if the law so allowed, we'd carry out direct -- we'd issue direct indictments for crimes which were not so serious, naturally if we had sufficient evidence. But in the case of grave crimes, we would institute investigations or, rather, we would suggest that the court conduct an investigation. At the time, the court -- or rather, the investigative judge conducted an investigation upon receiving a suggestion from the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That distinction between grave crimes that would cause you to request an investigation, could you elaborate on that a little bit more. What types of crimes would you have to request an investigation of an investigative judge and what types of crimes would you yourself institute or proffer an indictment?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Well, it depended on the -- the sentence envisaged for individual crimes. For example, in the case of crimes which could be given a sentence of between three and five years, I couldn't tell you precisely now, because the law was amended on number of occasions and it was made more severe at the time, in relation to the law in force in peacetime, but we ourselves could decide in such cases whether we would accuse a person or not. For other crimes, which were subject to a sentence of over three or five year, we had to carry out an investigation. And a full investigation would be launched by the court that had jurisdiction in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You indicated that reports were sometimes made to your office by brigades sometimes, by the military police and -- and from the corps. Which corps are you speaking of and which brigade -- brigades and which military police?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that from the beginning of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina and up until the end of the war there were numerous organisational changes implemented in the BH army. In fact, we only received reports from units that were part of the BH army. At the beginning, as far as I can remember, right up until the time when a transformation was implemented in 1993, there was the 3rd Corps and the brigades that formed part of the 3rd Corps, and there was the Zapad, or west operative group. After the transformation was made, the 7th Corps. was established, and we no longer had any points of contact -- we no longer had any contact with the 3rd Corps. As far as the corps is concerned, that's all I could say. But we most frequently received reports from the units in the Travnik municipality and the other municipalities that I have already mentioned. At the time, there was the 312th Brigade, then the 306th Brigade, the 17th Brigade, and brigades from neighbouring towns. For example, Jajce Brigade, the Novi Travnik Brigade, the Vitez and the Fojnica Brigade, et cetera, et cetera. There were seven or eight brigades that would file criminal reports with the district prosecutor's office in Travnik. This is what happened most frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These brigades that you just mentioned were parts of which corps? Can you recall?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part of the war they were part of the 7th Corps. I think that at the beginning of the war, up until the beginning or mid-1993, I think the corps concerned was the 3rd Corps. I can't exactly remember when the situation was transformed and when a new corps was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just for clarification, your answer is that the -- you received reports from the 3rd Corps and some of its brigades up until the point when the 7th Corps was established, but you can't remember exactly when the 7th Corps was established. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what was the official position, military position, of the persons in the brigade or the various brigades and the corps that you would usually receive reports from? And to clarify that, may I put it this way: Were there any military officials in the brigades or in the corps that had responsibility to forward to your office reports of criminal conduct by ABiH personnel?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. There were special sectors. There were so-called security services. And they would file criminal reports against people who had perpetrated crimes. There were also assistants in the brigades for legal affairs, and we would coordinate our activities with them. We'd cooperate with them in order to discover the perpetrators of various crimes in order to prosecute them. We would provide them with instructions and advice, since these were mostly young lawyers. We would tell them how to prepare a criminal report for further processing and how to provide all the relevant documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: After you received a report of a criminal offence from a brigade or from the corps, what was the role, if any, of the brigade or the corps in any future proceedings?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Well, it didn't have any particular role in the proceedings, unless the report was not quite complete. If its quality was poor, in such cases we would ask for further clarifications and for additional information, or we would contact the persons who had filed the report in order to clarify certain issues and to obtain additional information that would allow us to institute the criminal proceedings in a satisfactory manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: During your tenure as district prosecutor for Travnik, particularly in the years 1993 and 1994, or focus solely on the year 1993, approximately how many reports of criminal offences or cases did you receive?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to say exactly now, given the amount of time that has passed. I've been a prosecutor from that time right up until today, and I work on various reports on a daily basis. But on average, during the wartime period we would receive between 700 and 900 reports against individuals, and I am referring to individuals, not cases. Those are the records that we had. But to be more precise with respect to 1993, I really couldn't be more precise with respect to the year 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And can you give us an approximate breakdown as to how many of these cases would be cases that would have to be forwarded, as it were, to the investigative judge for further investigations and how many -- or what proportion you would institute indictments?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Well, to provide you with percentages now would be very difficult without having access to certain reports and to other relevant information. As far as I can remember, I think that it was about -- the proportion was about 50/50. I would say that about 50 per cent of the cases -- for 50 per cent of the cases direct indictments were issued; whereas for another 50 per cent the matter would be referred to the investigative judge in order for further investigations to be conducted. But I really couldn't provide you with very precise information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you tell us what types of cases were -- withdrawn. Of the cases that your office had to deal with, what were the major crimes or what crimes constituted a major proportion of the reports that you had to deal with?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Do you mean in terms of the number of persons reported?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Well, on the whole, the largest number of persons reported were reported for crimes against the armed forces. There were over 40 per cent -- they constitute over 40 per cent of the people concerned. Then there were crimes that had to do with property, theft, aggravated theft, burglary; they accounted for 15 to 20 per cent of all the criminal reports. Then there were criminal reports that concerned crimes against natural persons. For example, murder. And then there were various other types of crimes from all the various fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Briefly, if you can in a sentence, tell us what you mean when you say, "There were crimes against the armed forces." What are those crimes?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Well, this concerned desertion, not obeying officers, not responding to summonses, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in respect to crimes against property, could you just elaborate on that a little bit. What did those crimes involve?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Theft, aggravated theft, burglary, deceit, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the persons that were accused, did they generally speaking belong to any particular organisation? Or may I put it this way: Did they generally speaking belong to any particular unit or formation?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 99 per cent of the cases, they were part of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The victims, with respect to the crimes against property, can you remember if they were from any one or more ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Well, they were members of various ethnic groups; although, I would say that most of the victims, most of the injured persons were Bosniaks. They belonged to the ethnic group of Bosniaks or the ethnic group of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How about crimes against a person? Can you say anything about the ethnic origin of the victims that you -- in respect to the reports that you received?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as crimes against persons are concerned, this concerned Bosniaks mostly, with the exception of one or two cases. In these cases, the persons concerned were Serbs or Croats. But in all the other cases, the persons concerned were Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stamp, it would be best to have the break now, since it is quarter to 4.00. We'll have a 25-minute break and we will resume at ten past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Travnik district military court you said was set up in December 1992. For how long was it operational?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: It was operational throughout the war, that is, until the beginning of 1996, when it was abolished by a special law; that is, both the district military court and district military prosecutors throughout the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, the area controlled by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know where the records relating to matters that it had dealt with were kept?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: The legal successor of the district military court was the higher court in Zenica, and then later, with the establishment of cantonal prosecutor's offices and courts, these courts and prosecutor's offices took all the records over. In the case of Travnik, it is the canton district court and the canton prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall whether the Travnik district military court prosecuted any ABiH soldiers for the burning of Croat houses during 1993, 1994, 1995, 1996?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall if you received any reports from ABiH military units about ABiH soldiers being involved in burning Croat homes?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: I never received any such report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the district military court prosecute any ABiH soldiers for any war crimes or crimes against humanity, and did you receive any report against any ABiH soldiers for those offences?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, for such offences or crimes I did not receive criminal reports from anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: More specifically, did your office or the district military court receive reports of crimes of murder committed against Croat civilians or HVO soldiers by ABiH troops?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I think that there were very few such reports against members of soldiers of the ABiH because of killing HVO soldiers, but I think we did receive a report against three soldiers who killed a Croat civilian in the area of Turbe in the Travnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall any report that you received in respect of ABiH soldiers killing prisoners of war or any prisoner at all?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: We never received any such report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you receive any report alleging that ABiH soldiers mistreated HVO prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: I never received any such report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you receive any reports of -- alleging that ABiH soldiers mistreated civilian prisoners in custody in any particular place?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect, I never received any such report, nor am I aware of any civilians being held in any place within the territory of the prosecutor's office for which we had authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours. I have nothing further of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I now give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Zeric.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in connection with your oral ruling regarding the duration of the cross-examination, I should kindly request that we be allowed longer time for this witness than used by the Prosecution for this witness, as this is a witness who can provide the Court with important information on measures taken, and those measures taken are an essential element of command responsibility. So I think that the Defence has a special interest in cross-examining this witness about those matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you know, there are two Defence teams plus -- which means that you have 50 per cent more than the time envisaged. If you go beyond that, we will see. In any event, the Judges may also have questions for this witness, but you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zeric, my name is Edina Residovic, and I am Defence counsel for General Hadzihasanovic. Let me start immediately with questions so that we can make the best of the time that we have at our disposal. In answer to a question from my learned friend you said that you were prosecutor of the district military court in Travnik from the 22nd of December, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you held that position until those district prosecutor's offices were abolished, and that was in February 1996; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After the district military prosecutor's office was abolished in 1996, you performed the duties of municipal prosecutor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: No. After that, I was deputy of the higher prosecutor in Zenica, until September -- or rather, until the end of 1996. And after that, I was appointed Deputy Minister of Justice in the government of the Central Bosnian canton in 1997 and 1998. As of 1999 until the end of 2003, I was municipal prosecutor in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, as during the examination-in-chief it was noted in the record that from 1995 until the beginning of the war you performed various duties in Travnik. Would it be correct to say that it was from 1985 until the beginning of the war that you held various duties?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Yes, roughly. That is the period I meant. I don't remember the exact dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I just made the correction because of the transcript, where the year was incorrectly noted. You said that you were elected deputy district prosecutor in Banja Luka. Is it true, Mr. Zeric, that for the last two years a major reform of the judicial system is underway so that all the personnel, both prosecutors and judges, have been subject to detailed review?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The election to positions of prosecutors and judges was done by a special commission; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Those commissions, in addition to domestic lawyers, international lawyers, judges, prosecutors, and other prominent international experts are members; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The presidents of the independent commissions are also foreigners.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, you applied for the position of deputy prosecutor in Banja Luka, and after the procedure you were nominated to that position; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were appointed, rather.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As for a number of years you were a prosecutor, I believe that you are very familiar with criminal law and legal proceedings, so that I have a few questions for you in that area. Is it true to say that district military prosecutor's offices were formed by a decree with a force of law in August 1992? That decree --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So these district prosecutor's offices were formed on the 13th of August, 1992 but that decree did not envisage the existence of a military prosecutor's office in Travnik, so that it was amended in November 1992 when this particular prosecutor's office was established; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: I can't confirm that with certainty, but I do know that the district prosecutor's office -- military prosecutor's office and court was formed in the autumn of 1992 and that I was appointed on the 22nd of December. I know that for sure. Now, whether the actual wording of the law envisaged this or was it through subsequent amendments, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the decree with the force of law on military prosecutor's offices. We have copies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is probably a copy that is authentic and identical with the original, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This decree, item 4, did not make provision for a district military prosecutor's office in Travnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: That is what the article says.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, the decree did regulate the main competencies of the prosecutor and his legal position; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Yes, in items 5 and onwards -- Article 5 and onwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in view of the fact that we haven't managed to translate the amended decree of the 10th of November, 1992, which regulates the existence of the district court in Travnik, we believe that it is of interest for these proceedings for the B/C/S version to be shown to the witness, as it is brief. He can read it out. And we will provide a translation of that decree subsequently. Could the witness be handed a copy in the B/C/S language, that is, the amended decree on the district military prosecutor's office, which provides for the formation of a district prosecutor's office in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zeric, would you be kind enough to read Article 1, as it only has two articles, so that the amendment to the previous-mentioned decree on district public prosecutor's office may be recorded.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: "Decree with law of force are being added two paragraphs: The district military court in Gorazde and Livno, as well as Travnik to cover the territory of the district military court in Travnik."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zeric, do you recognise these decrees with the force of law on the basis of which the public prosecutor's office, of which you were the prosecutor, was formed?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the decrees on the basis of which we operated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as the witness is familiar with these laws, and they were published in the Official Gazette, I should like to tender both documents into evidence as Defence exhibits. And the Defence promises to provide an English translation of the amendment to the decree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stamp, regarding this document, which might have been tendered by the Prosecution as well, which should have been tendered, actually, what are your remarks regarding the Defence request for the admission of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, will you give these documents exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the decree on the law on military prosecution -- military prosecutor's offices will have the exhibit number DH115, and the English version DH115/E; and the exhibit titled, "Amended decree on the military district prosecutor's office," dated 10th November 1992 will have exhibit numbers DH116 and the English version, when tendered, will be DH116/E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zeric, is it true that the competencies of your prosecutor's office covered the municipalities of Travnik, Gornji Vakuf, Jajce, Vitez, Novi Travnik, Busovaca, Fojnica, and Kiseljak, which corresponded to the competencies of the district military court in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that already by the end of 1992 most of the municipalities of Donji Vakuf and Jajce fell into the hands of the Serb forces so that you were not able to perform your prosecutor's duties?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that at the beginning of 1993 and in accordance with the request of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna on the formation of parallel organs of authority, that courts and prosecutor's offices of the HVO were formed which were operational in Travnik until June 1993, upon which they moved to Vitez? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in the first half of 1993 there were two prosecutor's bodies, that is, the district military prosecutor's office, which you headed, and the prosecutor's office of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. But also there was the basic public prosecutor's office for civilian affairs that was housed in the same building.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Zeric, that by the spring of 1993 the HVO had full control over the municipalities of Kiseljak, Busovaca, Vitez, and most of the municipality of Novi Travnik, parts of municipality of Fojnica so that you were not able to perform your prosecutor's duties in the territories of these municipalities?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: It is true that they had control over these -- parts of these territories. To what extent, I really don't know. But wherever the HVO had control, we were unable to perform the duties of prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you will agree with me, Mr. Zeric, if I say that the military police and its security organs and the prosecutor's office, as a part of this institution, could not undertake any measures in the territories under the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: No civilian or military body had any authority in territories controlled by the HVO in that time period.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have already said, if I understood you correctly, that the district military prosecutor's office and the military court in Travnik had real competence for the prosecution of members of the army for all kinds of criminal offences; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, in answer to another question I put to you, you said that there was also a basic prosecutor's office in Travnik as well as a basic prosecutor's office in Bugojno; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Both these prosecutor's offices, in accordance with the law, prosecuted perpetrators of criminal offences that envisaged a sentence up to ten years; whereas for worse crimes, the higher prosecutor's office in Zenica was responsible.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Yes, exclusively for civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war, the basic and higher prosecutor's offices had competencies over all persons but with the passing of this decree on district public prosecutor's offices there was a separation of competencies in view of the nature of the perpetrators; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, yes. But before the war, there were also military tribunals attached to the former Yugoslav army, and they were competent for certain offences.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Quite right. They were competent for military personnel who committed acts against the armed forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, the procedure in district military courts and the acts of the prosecutor's offices were guided by the Law on Criminal Procedure of the SFRY, which Bosnia and Herzegovina took over as its own in 1992.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Yes. We worked fully in accordance with the Criminal Code and the Law on Criminal Procedure of the former SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When talking about the Criminal Code, which regulated material criminal offences, that is, stipulated the criminal offences for which persons may be prosecuted, you applied the criminal law of the SFRY, which was taken over by Bosnia and Herzegovina as its own, and which contained certain general elements of responsibility and crimes and specific crimes, and in addition, you applied the law of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which regulated the remaining criminal offences; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Yes. We acted in accordance with the laws you have mentioned, which were taken over by decree and became the laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of 1992, the Presidency on a number of occasions, as you noted a moment ago, took certain decisions to amend the existing laws; however, not one of those amendments changed the position of the prosecutor in the criminal proceedings. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In that period of time, like the other judicial entities, you were in a rather difficult situation because Sarajevo was under siege and legal regulations and acts from Sarajevo and towards Sarajevo couldn't really travel. It was not possible to deliver them.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: This was partially true. But we managed using various channels and fax machines to receive certain regulations with a great deal of delay. That is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, to ensure the unhindered functioning of the judiciary, in Zenica in mid-1993 a department of the Supreme Court was set up to deal with appeals against rulings of courts outside Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you already told me that military prosecutor's offices had certain competencies, as stipulated by the Penal Code and the decree on public prosecutor's offices, I should like to ask you to assist the Chamber in a better understanding of your role to confirm for me whether I am right in saying that your competencies were to be an organ of the judiciary, rather than an organ of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were an organ of the judiciary, and this is corroborated by the fact that regular courts at the second instance also prosecuted the same crimes as we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The material obligations toward the district military prosecutor's office and the district court was in the hands of the Ministry of Justice; whereas, administrative affairs were regulated by the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: SEAD ZERIC
